cooked:
Have you ever noticed — no theory truly begins from nothing. Every doctrine, every explanation, starts with an axiom: a foundational assumption, an article of belief we accept without proof. It lies outside logic, beyond questioning, not because it’s irrefutable — but because we choose to treat it as the ground from which all else can grow.

We are taught to “believe” these axioms — not to prove them, but to trust them. Upon these initial leaps of faith, logic constructs vast architectures. One layer supports the next, and those “superstructures” give rise to even more complex frameworks — “super-superstructures,” if you will — until eventually, we declare: We understand.

But what is this process, really?
Is learning just the act of finding the missing links between ideas we’ve already agreed to believe in? Is it the acceptance of new connections as long as they don’t threaten the foundations we’ve inherited?

And so the question deepens:
Do we ever truly learn anything new?
Or are we simply wandering the corridors of an already-built palace, discovering rooms we hadn’t noticed before — rooms built atop assumptions we never laid ourselves?

Is there anything new to learn — or only new ways to believe?

I think learning is understanding relationship between different things. Observing how they are connected. How one affects other and so on and understanding the complete cycle of that chain. At the last how it affects us.

It’s like observing movement of information between entities in relationship.

This post reminds me of a famous Carl Sagan quote - If you wish to make an apple pie from scratch, you must first invent the universe.

I suppose this applies to learning something from scratch too.

This brings to mind the following (slightly abridged) phrase attributed to Albert Einstein:
As the circle of light grows, so does the circumference of darkness surrounding it.

Every formal system requires axioms — unproven, assumed truths. In mathematics, these are explicit (e.g., Euclid’s postulates). In science, they’re often implicit: the uniformity of nature, the reliability of observation. Even reason itself — logic — rests on principles we don’t prove so much as presume (like the law of non-contradiction). However, this isn’t a flaw; it’s a necessity.
Without these starting points, one falls into an infinite regress of justifications — every proof needing a proof needing a proof. So we need to anchor our reasoning in something unprovable, not because it’s immune to doubt, but because it’s where our inquiry must begin.

Baskaran_Nadar:

Is learning just the act of finding the missing links between ideas we’ve already agreed to believe in? Is it the acceptance of new connections as long as they don’t threaten the foundations we’ve inherited?

I think, to some extent, yes. Much of what we call learning is interpretation within a system: learning to think “correctly” within a worldview. We connect dots, fill in blanks, build models. But occasionally — rarely — something deeper shifts: the axioms themselves are challenged. This is paradigm change. Revolutions in thought don’t just add new rooms to the palace — they knock down walls, question the foundation, and sometimes rebuild.

Baskaran_Nadar:

Do we ever truly learn anything new?

If learning means adding new facts within the same frame, then yes — constantly. If it means stepping outside the frame itself, questioning the axioms, shifting the bedrock — that’s rarer, more destabilizing, but also more transformative.

Baskaran_Nadar:

Is there anything new to learn — or only new ways to believe?

Maybe it’s not a palace, but a labyrinth — built on beliefs, yes, but not static. A living architecture, reshaping itself when brave minds ask not just what do we know, but why do we believe it?
